newsitem.title: USA: Congresswoman pushes bill on mastectomies.
newsitem.headline: Congresswoman pushes bill on mastectomies.

text.p: A Republican Congresswoman vowed Friday to push legislation requiring insurers to provide at least 48 hours of hospital care for mastectomy patients, calling industry efforts to address the issue insufficient.

"Health maintenance organizations seem to be making a concentrated attack on the health concerns of women," New Jersey Rep. Marge Roukema said in a statement. "I will not settle for third-world standards for health care for women in this country, and neither will the 184,000 women who contract breast cancer each year."

Roukema said she would join forces next year with Connecticut Democrat Rosa DeLauro, who had previously introduced a bill requiring 48 hours of inpatient care following a mastectomy. The addition of the New Jersey Republican could increase political momentum for the bill.

Anticipating a possible move in Congress to set hospital standards for mastectomies, officials of large managed-care plans announced Thursday a new policy calling for at least one night's stay for women who undergo the procedure.
The American Association of Health Plans, a major trade group, said health maintenance organizations should not require that women who have a breast removed get only outpatient coverage.

Recently issued medical guidelines say some women may do well with only outpatient care for the procedure. Opponents say a number of managed-care plans are limiting coverage for the procedure, but it is unclear how many.

The American Cancer Association commended the group for its action, saying it believed "treatment decisions for women with breast cancer should be made by the physician in consultation with the patient."

The managed-care officials admitted they were hoping voluntary action would head off legislation in Congress. Lawmakers have shown they are ready and willing to address public concerns about managed care.

Earlier this year, Congress passed and President Clinton signed into law legislation requiring insurers to cover at least 48 hours of hospital care for new mothers after a normal delivery and 96 hours after a Cesarean section.
The new law came in response to information that managed-care plans were allowing only 24-hour coverage, and in some cases as little as 12 hours, after routine deliveries.
